description: We’re MyWorkInMafia, a six-person team from Peru. Several of us have worked together at MyWorkIn, and we bring skills in software development, applied AI, data analysis, and product design. We chose Flame in Freefall because we’re curious about how fire behaves in microgravity. Our team is full, and we’d love to connect with others interested in combustion science, experimental data, and scientific visualization.
summary:
FireFist is a web dashboard built on NASA's PSI combustion data. The user picks one of six destinations: an Earth lab, the ISS, a lunar habitat, a pressurized rover, a transit vehicle or a Mars habitat. Each destination sets an atmosphere (oxygen, pressure), a gravity level and an airflow. The dashboard then lists the PSI tests closest to those conditions, ranks the 24 combustion investigations for them, and shows which combinations of fuel, oxygen, pressure and airflow have no test in PSI. An AI copilot operates the dashboard and answers with citations to document pages.

Each value is labeled as measured, extracted from a document (with quote and page) or assumed. Two results come out of this: no solid fuel in PSI's experiment tables was tested above 22.2 % oxygen, while NASA is considering 26.5 % to 34 % oxygen for Moon and Mars surfaces; and interpolating between 0 g and 1 g does not bound flammability at partial gravity.
details:
What it does

  • Closest tests: for the chosen destination, the PSI tests nearest to its conditions, with fuel, sample shape and size, oxygen, pressure, airflow and sensors. Real PSI video plays for the tests that have it.
  • Ranking: the 24 combustion investigations ordered by relevance to the destination. The weights are visible, and a robustness analysis shows which positions hold when the weights change.
  • Gaps: combinations of fuel, material, oxygen, pressure and airflow with no test in PSI. A gap is always worded as "no tests in PSI", and what exists outside PSI is listed apart.
  • Findings: more than 100 reviewed findings from PSI documents, each with its conditions, a verbatim quote, the page and the figure. The sentence shown is generated from a template, not written by a model.
  • Equipment: fire-safety equipment and controls grouped as prevention, detection and suppression, with applications on Earth.
  • Flame view: a 3D flame for the selected conditions, labeled as an illustrative model and not as a result.
  • Export: CSV with a data version, a column dictionary and BibTeX/RIS citations.
  • Guided tours: AI-guided walkthroughs that move the camera, set the scenario and open the relevant view.

How it works

A script downloads PSI's tables and documents and normalizes 22 experiment tables (more than 2,000 rows). Roughly 13,500 test conditions were extracted from reports; each keeps its file, page and a quote that was checked against the source text. A deterministic engine written in TypeScript computes coverage, ranking and comparisons. The copilot does not calculate: it calls the same tools the interface uses (more than 20, for example flying to a destination, querying tests, showing the limit map or searching documents) and reports what they return. A retrieval service answers qualitative questions from document pages and returns "not found" when no page supports an answer. A number checker compares the figures in the copilot's answers with the data.

Users

  • Researchers: filtered queries, errata of PSI's own tables, provenance per value, export.
  • Aerospace engineers: a passport per destination with atmosphere and gravity, the ranking, equipment and gaps.
  • Professors and students: guided tours that go from a question to the supporting data and video.

What it does not do

It does not simulate combustion and does not extrapolate between fuel types. Partial-gravity results are shown as interpolations, never as measurements.

Goals

  • Let an engineer check what PSI supports before relying on a material or an atmosphere.
  • Let a researcher cite and reuse a value with its source.
  • Let a student follow a question to its data.

Tools

Next.js, React, TypeScript, three.js, CopilotKit, Python and Node data pipelines, a Python document-retrieval service, Playwright and Vitest for tests, Blender for the illustrative models. The LLM provider is configurable; the default is Anthropic. Code is MIT-licensed and derived data is CC0.
